issues.explanation: The trigger set suggests a highly specific external threat context involving cyclists and thrown objects, but the rest of the profile (memory and appraisals) does not contain corresponding content about that kind of event. In a man-made disaster profile, 'burnt smell' coheres with disaster-related sensory memory, whereas 'people cycling' and 'throwing objects' pull toward a different trauma scenario and are hard to integrate with the remaining items.

'Avoid seeing friends' is not well supported by the rest of the selected profile. The active formulation strongly links Triggers with Memory and Maladaptive Strategies, and the endorsed strategies are otherwise cognitive/internal (thought avoidance, thought monitoring). Social avoidance could occur in PTSD, but here it is not tied to any endorsed trigger, memory content, or appraisal pattern, making it look like a strategy for a different symptom cluster than the one described.

vignette:
When Carlos was fifty-three, he had been working as a counselor at a community mental health center for nearly two decades. He was good at his job-able to sit with clients in their worst moments and help them find a way through. On the day of the disaster, he was leading an afternoon anger management group. A client, a younger man whose case had been particularly difficult, had been escalating for weeks. That afternoon, the man stood up mid-session, picked up a metal chair from the circle, and hurled it at the wall beside Carlos. It missed his head by inches. Then the client overturned a table, sending papers and a coffee mug flying. In the chaos, a small electrical fire started in the corner where a lamp had been knocked over. The smell of burning wiring and melting plastic filled the room before the sprinklers came on. By the time the fire was out and the client was restrained, Carlos was standing in the soaked room, shaking, his ears ringing. He told himself it was over and that he was fine. But he wasn't.

Over the months that followed, that burned smell became a constant companion in ways he had not anticipated. It was not just external triggers that got him-a neighbor's barbecue, a candle left too long, the scent of toast burning-but also times when no smell was present at all. Lying in bed at night, his mind would drift, and suddenly he would be back in that room, the acrid odor of hot plastic and scorched wiring filling his nostrils as vividly as if the fire had just happened. The smell came with no warning, and it brought the whole scene flooding in: the crash of the chair, the hiss of the sprinklers, the terror of being helpless. He would sit up, gasping, certain the apartment was burning, even though everything was quiet and dark. Each time his nostrils caught that acrid note-whether from the outside world or from his own memory-his body reacted before his mind could catch up: heart hammering, palms slick, jaw clenched. He had come to believe that his body was his enemy, that it refused to accept that he was safe. Even sitting alone in his apartment, he would feel a wave of terror wash over him without any clear image attached; he would be flooded with the full emotional force of that afternoon-the helplessness, the suddenness-while the smell of burnt wiring filled his senses, though there was nothing burning anywhere nearby. The memory felt distant when he did try to grasp it, like something that had happened to another person, someone he was watching in a film. But the feeling-and the smell-was all his.

He began to monitor his own thoughts with exhausting vigilance. Carlos was certain that if he let his mind wander anywhere near that day, he would unravel completely. So he became a kind of sentinel inside his own head, scanning for any drift, any stray image or smell, and slamming the door shut before it could take hold. At work, where his days were spent listening to other people's stories of trauma, he found himself avoiding any client who talked about violence or fires, even though he had once been skilled at exactly those cases. He stopped attending the monthly staff meetings where colleagues sometimes debriefed difficult incidents, worried that someone would bring up that day. When a coworker asked how he was doing, he gave a curt "fine" and walked away.

His social life evaporated. He had always been someone who met friends for dinner or a drink on weekends, but now he found excuses-he was tired, he had paperwork, he had a cold. The truth was that he could not bear the unpredictability of being around others. What if someone threw something in a disagreement? What if a restaurant kitchen had a smoky grill? He had to be especially careful, he told himself, because you never knew what could happen next. The world felt like a place where disaster was hiding around every corner, and only constant scanning could keep him safe. The isolation took its toll. His closest friend called twice, then stopped. Carlos spent most evenings alone in his apartment, eating microwaved meals, the television on low to fill the silence, but his attention was always half-cocked, listening for a siren, waiting for something to go wrong-or for that phantom smell to creep back into his awareness, reminding him that his own mind was a place where the fire still burned.

What finally brought him to therapy was a night when a car backfired outside his window. He dove to the floor, his hands over his head, and stayed there for nearly an hour, sobbing, unable to get up. The next morning he called a colleague he trusted and asked for a referral. Sitting in the intake office, he told the psychologist he was tired of being afraid all the time, but what he really wanted to know was whether he was going crazy. He said he couldn't keep living like this, with his own mind and body turned against him, but he was terrified that if he let himself think about that day, even once, he would fall apart and never get put back together.
